clinicalPearls: A segmental form of porokeratosis presenting as linear, Blaschko-distributed plaques with the characteristic raised keratotic border (cornoid lamella)
It represents a mosaic manifestation, often reflecting a post-zygotic second hit in the mevalonate-pathway genes that also cause the generalised inherited porokeratoses
Dermoscopy and histology show the cornoid lamella, a column of parakeratosis marking the advancing edge
Lesions typically begin in infancy or childhood and follow the lines of Blaschko along a limb
It carries the highest malignant potential of the porokeratosis variants, with squamous cell carcinoma and Bowen disease arising within long-standing plaques
Extensive or facial linear porokeratosis may rarely coexist with skeletal or developmental anomalies, warranting broader assessment
Management is generic: sun protection, topical keratolytics or field therapies, and long-term surveillance with biopsy of any suspicious change
reference.pathophysiology: Linear porokeratosis is regarded as a mosaic disorder in which a post-zygotic second hit occurs in a cell already carrying a germline variant in the mevalonate biosynthetic pathway, most often affecting genes such as MVK, PMVK, MVD or FDPS. Loss of function in this pathway within the affected clone disturbs epidermal keratinocyte proliferation and differentiation, producing the cornoid lamella, a column of abnormal parakeratotic cells that defines the advancing border of each lesion. Because the second hit occurs during development, the lesions are distributed along the lines of Blaschko. The clonal, genetically unstable epidermis explains the heightened risk of malignant transformation within these plaques.
additionalDifferentials: Other porokeratosis variants (porokeratosis of Mibelli, disseminated superficial actinic porokeratosis)
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy to demonstrate the cornoid lamella and exclude malignancy
Dermoscopy to identify the characteristic peripheral keratotic ridge
Serial photography to monitor for change
Biopsy of any nodular, ulcerated or rapidly changing area
Skeletal or developmental assessment where lesions are extensive or facial
Molecular testing for mevalonate-pathway variants where available
redFlags: Nodule, ulceration or bleeding within a plaque suggesting squamous cell carcinoma
Rapid enlargement of a previously stable lesion
Extensive disease with associated skeletal or developmental anomalies
Non-healing erosion within a long-standing lesion
reference.prognosis: The condition is chronic and persistent; while many lesions remain stable, linear porokeratosis has the greatest malignant potential among the porokeratoses, so lifelong surveillance is warranted and prognosis worsens if squamous cell carcinoma develops.
pitfalls: Dismissing linear keratotic plaques as an epidermal naevus and missing the cornoid lamella
Failing to biopsy a changing lesion because porokeratosis was assumed benign
Underestimating the malignant potential of the linear variant
Neglecting sun protection, which accelerates malignant change
references: Happle R. Mosaicism in Human Skin
management: No definitive cure exists; management centres on lesion control and vigilant malignancy surveillance because this variant carries the highest malignant potential of the porokeratoses

Topical therapies for symptomatic lesions include topical retinoids, topical 5-fluorouracil and vitamin D analogues, with topical cholesterol-statin combinations directed at the underlying mevalonate-pathway defect
Advise strict photoprotection to limit keratinocyte damage and reduce the risk of malignant transformation
Undertake regular skin surveillance with serial photography and biopsy any nodular, ulcerated or rapidly changing area to detect squamous cell carcinoma or Bowen disease early
Use cryotherapy, laser or surgical excision for localised, symptomatic or suspicious lesions
Arrange skeletal and developmental assessment where lesions are extensive or facial
Escalate to surgical excision and oncological management if squamous cell carcinoma develops within a plaque
